title: Users and sessions
description: Replay a real account setup on a Debian 13 server: useradd, passwd, groupadd and usermod, the lines they write to /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow and /etc/group, su and sudo, and who is logged in with w, who, last and wtmpdb last.
intro: Jonas starts at TuxPixel today. Mira creates his account on the build server, and you replay what each command printed and changed. Watch the account files after every step: most of these commands print nothing when they succeed.
takeaways: `useradd -m -s /bin/bash name` creates the account, its home directory (filled from `/etc/skel`) and, on Debian, a private group of the same name. Without `-m`, no home directory is made.

`/etc/passwd` is readable by everyone and holds name, `x`, UID, GID, comment, home and shell. The password hashes live in `/etc/shadow`, which only root can read; `!` there means no password is set yet.

`passwd name` (as root) sets someone else's password without asking for the old one. `groupadd group` creates a group; `usermod -aG group name` adds a supplementary group, and without `-a` it would replace them all.
`id` shows UID, GID and groups. `su - user` asks for that user's password and starts a login shell; `sudo` asks for your own password and runs one command as root, and `sudo -i` opens a root shell.

`who` lists the users logged in now, and `w` adds what each one is doing and the system's load. `last` lists past logins from the login records; on Debian 13 that job moved to `wtmpdb last`, and the wtmpdb package also provides `last`.

links.title: Debian 13 release notes: last, lastb and lastlog are replaced

scenes.title: Create the account
scenes.text: Mira checks her own groups, then creates Jonas's account with a home directory and bash as his shell.

notes.id-mira: Membership in `sudo` is what lets Mira run commands as root.
notes.useradd: No output: on success, useradd says nothing.
notes.home-denied: Debian 13 creates home directories that only their owner can open, so Mira needs `sudo` to look inside.

questions.prompt: Which shell will Jonas get when he logs in?
questions.why: The last field of the `/etc/passwd` line is the login shell, set with `-s`. The field before it is the home directory.

questions.prompt: Where did the files in Jonas's new home directory come from?
distractors: They were copied from Mira's home
bash created them at his first login
questions.why: With `-m`, useradd copies the skeleton directory into the new home: the same three files, now owned by Jonas.

scenes.title: Set a password
scenes.text: The new account can't log in yet. Mira looks at its shadow entry, sets a password, and looks again.

notes.passwd: Run by root (here through sudo), passwd doesn't ask for Jonas's old password. Nothing appears as the new one is typed.
notes.shadow-set: The second field is now a hash of the password, never the password itself; `$y$` marks the yescrypt method.

questions.answer: Only root may read it, because it holds the password hashes
distractors: The file is empty until a password is set
It is locked while useradd runs
questions.why: `/etc/passwd` is world-readable; the hashes moved to `/etc/shadow` so that ordinary users can't copy them.

questions.prompt: What does the `!` in Jonas's first shadow line mean?
questions.answer: No usable password is set, so he can't log in with one
distractors: His password is an exclamation mark
questions.why: useradd leaves the password field locked. After `passwd`, a hash takes its place.

scenes.title: Groups
scenes.text: Jonas will share artwork with the other artists, so Mira creates a group and adds him to it.

notes.usermod: `-a` appends: without it, `-G` would replace all of Jonas's supplementary groups.

questions.prompt: In `/etc/group`, where does Jonas appear as a member of `artists`?
questions.answer: In the last field of the `artists` line
distractors: In the third field of the `jonas` line
In the second field, instead of the `x`
questions.why: A group line is name, `x`, GID and the comma-separated list of supplementary members. Jonas's primary group, `jonas`, is recorded by GID in `/etc/passwd`.

scenes.title: Switching users
scenes.text: Mira checks that Jonas's password works with `su`, then opens a root shell with `sudo -i`.

notes.su: `su -` asks for Jonas's password, not Mira's, and starts a login shell in his home.
notes.sudo-i: No password prompt: sudo still remembered Mira's. The prompt ends in `#` while she is root.

questions.prompt: Whose password did `su - jonas` ask for?
questions.why: su asks for the password of the account you switch to. sudo asks for your own.

scenes.title: Who is logged in?
scenes.text: Ada is logged in over SSH from the laptop. Mira checks the current sessions and the login history.

notes.w: Ada is running `top`; the `?` under PCPU is how this capture showed it.
notes.last: The su and sudo -i sessions from the previous scene appear too, on `pts/1`.
notes.which-last: On Debian 13, `last` comes from the wtmpdb package: it is a link to `wtmpdb`, so both print the same.

questions.prompt: What does `w` show about Ada that `who` doesn't?
questions.answer: What she is running right now
questions.why: Both show the terminal, the time and where the login came from; `w` adds idle time, CPU use and the current command in the WHAT column.

questions.prompt: Which line of `last` is still going?
distractors: None: last only lists ended sessions
questions.why: `still logged in` marks a session that hasn't ended; the su and sudo sessions ended when Mira typed `exit`.
